zone: Kindy Creek, Found Creek and Illabot Creek — the Snowking and Buckindy peaks
_areas_note: THIS IS NOT CASCADE PASS. Every peak here is served by a spur that leaves the Cascade River Road far below the road end, or by a road out of Darrington on the other side of the massif. The main eastern trailhead is Forest Service road 1570, signed off the Cascade River Road about 14.2 miles up from Marblemount, which turns south, crosses the Cascade River and climbs toward Kindy Ridge; it is drivable only to around 1,300 feet and the rest is walked, with two substantial washouts at roughly three quarters of a mile and two miles in. That road serves both the Kindy Creek and Found Creek sides and is the standard way to Snowking Mountain, Mutchler Peak and Mount Buckindy. The western trailhead is the Slide Lake trail, reached by driving State Route 530 about 16 miles north from Darrington and then some 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, and it is the way to Snowking's west side; the same Illabot road, at the Arrow Creek switchback around 2,220 feet and roughly 16 miles in, is the start for Mount Chaval. All four peaks are in Glacier Peak Wilderness on Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, so nothing here is under North Cascades National Park rules and no in-person park permit is involved. Mount Buckindy and Snowking Mountain were removed from a Ptarmigan Traverse zone in an earlier pass because they are not traverse peaks, and that removal was correct: Buckindy drains north to the Cascade River by Kindy Creek and south to the Suiattle by Buck and Downey creeks, and its name is the two creeks run together, while Snowking sits further west again between Found Creek and Illabot Creek. Nothing on the traverse serves either of them and none of the traverse camps appear in this file. Mutchler Peak is the alpine high point of Snowking's long curving southeast ridge and shares the Kindy Ridge approach. Mount Chaval sits immediately southwest of Snowking and is the odd one out in that its standard approach is off Illabot Creek Road rather than the Cascade River Road, but it is the same wilderness, the same permits and the same brush, and it has no closer neighbour anywhere. No peak was excluded.

sites.name: Found Lake and the Kindy Ridge saddle
sites.capacity: A few rough spots by the lake, party-sized. Nothing established, no toilet, no platforms.
sites.water: The lake, dependable through the season, and the first certain water after the long walk up the old logging road. The saddle above it is dry.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue wilderness permit from the register. Forest Service road 1570 has no developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass is not normally required there, unlike the Slide Lake trail on the other side of the massif; confirm with the district before relying on that. Practical bear precautions are a hang or a canister rather than a requirement here, since this is not park ground.
sites.notes: The first useful camp on the eastern approach and the one most parties reach on a late start. From where road 1570 becomes impassable you walk the blocked, overgrown roadbed for roughly three miles, crossing several creeks and two large washouts that are genuinely awkward when snowmelt is high, then take a steep climbers' path off it at about 2,300 feet. That path leads up toward this lake, and the junction where the Found Lake line and the Snowking line split is in the saddle above at about 4,800 feet. Stopping here splits an approach that otherwise routinely takes two days and sometimes three. It is low, forested and buggy in early summer, and it is a long way still from any summit, so treat it as a staging camp rather than a base.

sites.name: Cyclone Lake and the lakes just north of it
sites.capacity: Unimproved sites around the small lakes north of Cyclone Lake, room for two or three parties. No toilet, nothing built.
sites.water: The lakes, reliable through the normal climbing season. This is the last certain water before the glacier and the ridge crest, and there is nothing running once you are up on the ice.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp back from the shoreline, use a stove rather than a fire at this elevation, and pack out what you bring in. No agency permit is reserved or quota'd anywhere in this zone, which is the practical difference from the park country up the road.
sites.notes: THE BASE CAMP FOR SNOWKING MOUNTAIN AND MUTCHLER PEAK, and the standard end of the Kindy Ridge approach. From the lakes the route follows the Kindy and Found ridge crest south-southwest above Cyclone Lake, keeping south of a cornice that overhangs the ridge, then turns west up moderately steep snow to the summit block; the alternative from the east side of the lake is heather and easy slabs up Snowking's east ridge, finishing on the south. Mutchler is the high point of the long curving ridge running southeast off Snowking and is reached along that crest, and the cirque between the two once held a substantial mid-elevation glacier of which only the highest north-facing ice remains. Getting here from the car is around thirty kilometres and two and a half thousand metres of cumulative gain by the time the undulating ridge is done, which is why nobody does this peak in a day. Snow lingers in the basin well into summer, which is when the camping is flattest and the water is easiest.

sites.name: Kindy Ridge crest camps
sites.capacity: Scattered heather benches and gravel flats along the crest rather than any one site, party-sized, spread over several miles of ridge. No facilities of any kind.
sites.water: Conditions-dependent and the thing to plan around. Early in the season there are snow patches and runnels most of the way along; by late summer whole sections of the crest are dry and the reliable water is back down at the lakes. Carry from the last certain source rather than expecting to find one.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on snow, rock or bare ground, keep off the heather where you can, and pack out human waste — there is no toilet anywhere in this zone. Stoves only up here.
sites.notes: The Kindy Ridge crest, also described as the northeast ridge, is a long undulating plod rather than a climb, and the honest description of camping on it is that parties stop where the day ends. There are quite a few workable spots and no established ones. This matters most for anyone linking the peaks rather than climbing one: the high route around the headwaters of Kindy Creek runs along this ground and Mutchler is often called the best vantage point on the whole traverse. Weather is the risk that makes a crest camp expensive here, since the ridge is exposed for miles with no shelter and the retreat is back down the same slow ground. Season is roughly July into September, earlier if you want continuous snow to travel on and later if you want the cornices gone.

sites.name: Head of Kindy Creek and the Kindy-Buck Creek pass
sites.capacity: One or two parties on snow, moraine or heather at the passes and in the basins beneath them. Nothing built, no toilet.
sites.water: Snowmelt and small basin streams, generally running through midsummer and thinning badly after that. There is ice on Buckindy's north and east flanks, so late in the season the water that is left is glacier outflow rather than clean snowmelt.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Camp on durable ground, pack out human waste, no fires. There is no quota and no reservation anywhere in this zone, so the constraint on a trip here is the approach rather than the paperwork.
sites.notes: THE GROUND THAT PUTS MOUNT BUCKINDY IN RANGE. Buckindy's standard route is a class 4 scramble on the north slopes, with glaciers on the north and east flanks, and the parties who climb it are camping either in the basins at the head of Kindy Creek or at the pass between the Kindy and Buck Creek drainages. Coming in from road 1570 this is a second or third night out, well beyond the Cyclone Lake ground. There is a second way in from the south, over Green Mountain and the Horse Lake saddle from the Suiattle side, with camps on the divide and in the basins on the way, but that country has its own long road problems and is not the approach this zone is built around. Nothing here is a site in any developed sense: it is remote, lightly visited ground where the answer to where you sleep is wherever the light runs out, and a party should carry the fuel to melt snow and the tolerance for a dry, windy night.

sites.name: Slide Lake
sites.capacity: Several rough sites, with the last good ones at about 1.25 miles where the well-beaten path ends. Parking at the trailhead takes roughly eight vehicles, which is a fair measure of how busy it gets.
sites.water: The lake and its inlet. Reliable, though the exposed lakebed in late summer is slick and muddy and the shallow edges are not pleasant to draw from.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit at the register, which is passed at about 0.9 miles where the boundary is marked. THIS IS THE ONLY OFFICIAL TRAILHEAD IN THE ZONE and so realistically the only place a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is needed on the vehicle. Camp back from the shore, stove rather than fire.
sites.notes: The western gateway, and by a long way the easiest walking in this file: about 2.5 miles round trip and 300 feet of gain to a lake formed when a landslide dammed the creek. For a climber it is a staging camp rather than an objective, since Snowking's west side and the lakes beyond are hours further on. Getting to the trailhead is the part to plan: from Darrington it is 16 miles north on the highway and then 20.5 miles up Illabot Creek Road, a long remote road with blind curves through the middle section and a small rock slide around mile 13.8 that can stop a low-clearance vehicle. Illabot Creek Road and the Cascade River Road have both been closed by washouts in the past and both are subject to seasonal closure, so confirm the road before committing to a trip that depends on it. The trail itself carries significant blowdown and boulder fields.

sites.name: Enjar Lake and Hamar Lake
sites.capacity: Unimproved lakeside spots for a party or two at either lake. No toilet, nothing established.
sites.water: Both lakes, dependable through the season. These are the last reliable water on the western approach before the ice.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit taken at the Slide Lake register. Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass on the vehicle at the Slide Lake trailhead. Camp back from the water, stoves only, pack out human waste.
sites.notes: The working camps on the western side of Snowking Mountain, reached by continuing past Slide Lake for roughly four hours of increasingly rough going. Either lake serves; parties pick whichever the light allows. From here Snowking is climbed on its west and northwest ground rather than by the east ridge and glacier line used from Cyclone Lake, which is the practical reason the two approaches are worth keeping apart. No elevations are recorded because no confident figures were found for either lake. This side is quieter than the Kindy Ridge side and correspondingly less travelled, so route-finding is on you and the boot path is intermittent to absent. Best from July into September, and expect wet brush on the way through regardless.

sites.name: Jug Lake
sites.capacity: Several good camps on the north side of the lake, roomy by the standards of this zone. Unimproved, no toilet.
sites.water: The lake, reliable. Nothing dependable above it once you are on the ridge and in the Arrow Creek amphitheatre.
sites.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue permit. Parking is at the Arrow Creek switchback on Illabot Creek Road rather than at a developed trailhead, so a vehicle pass may not apply there in the way it does at Slide Lake; check with the district rather than assume either way. No fires at the lake, and pack out human waste.
sites.notes: THE BASE FOR MOUNT CHAVAL, which sits immediately southwest of Snowking and has three standard approaches and one longer non-standard one, none of them simple and all of them brushy. This is the most used of them. Park at the prominent switchback where Arrow Creek meets Illabot Creek Road at about 2,220 feet, roughly 16 miles up the road, and follow an old overgrown fishermen's path up the right bank of Arrow Creek to the lake; it is reasonably defined and flagged at the doubtful places. From the camps on the north shore the route climbs north-northeast to gain the ridge around 5,200 feet, traverses to the pass between the two points just over 6,350 feet, and then commits to a genuine cross-country bushwhack through cliffy ground into the Arrow Creek amphitheatre before steep hillsides and talus lead to the mountain. Reckon on about ten miles and 4,600 feet for the round trip from the road, and on the vegetation being the crux. No elevation is recorded for the lake because no confident figure was found.
